findings.area: wp20_metric_visit_page_guard (UPDATE/DELETE immutability) together with issueMetricVisitPage INSERT per render
findings.issue: Anyone without authentication can make the server insert permanent rows, and nothing limits how many.
findings.evidence: issueMetricVisitPage runs on every dynamic render (connection() opts out of static/cached rendering). Each call inserts a row into LiveMetricVisitPage. The guard rejects every UPDATE and DELETE unless the parent LiveMetricVersion row is gone, and TRUNCATE is blocked. In the supplied code, nothing applies a rate limit, quota or retention to page issuance. The HTTP rate controls that were described only cover the prepare/collect endpoints.
findings.impact: Repeated GETs, bots or prefetches against a public live page add rows to the table and its two indexes, and each request opens its own write transaction. Expired rows can never be cleaned up without deleting the metric version, which also deletes the statistics. This gives an attacker a cheap way to grow storage and load connections and the DB, and it hurts the availability of the public page.
findings.recommended_fix: Bound issuance before the INSERT, for example with a per-client or per-scope limit or a cap on unexpired rows per version. Alternatively, add a narrowly guarded purge path for rows that expired and were never matched (no visit intent with the same scoped event), run by the owner only and documented as removing UNCOUNTED expectations only. If immutability until version deletion has to stay, record this as an approved risk and add monitoring of the table size.
findings.required_test: On a disposable DB, render or issue N expectations in a loop and confirm that the limit or purge behavior works. If you add a purge, confirm it deletes only expired, unmatched rows and still rejects matched or unexpired rows and direct arbitrary deletes.

findings.area: issueMetricVisitPage catch block / INSERT vs trigger lifetime check
findings.issue: When the trigger rejects the scope or lifetime, the error becomes PERSISTENCE_UNAVAILABLE, so the page crashes instead of rendering normally without the collector.
findings.evidence: The trigger takes issuedAt from clock_timestamp() later than resolveMetricVisitContext read the clock. It then raises SQLSTATE 23514 if collection is disabled, if collectionStartedAt > issuedAt, if NEW.expiresAt > version.expiresAt, or if expiresAt <= issuedAt. That error comes back as a Prisma error, not a MetricVisitorError, so the catch throws PERSISTENCE_UNAVAILABLE. Only SCOPE_UNAVAILABLE and LIFETIME_UNAVAILABLE return null.
findings.impact: A render that lands right at version or page expiry gets a 500 error and loses the public page, when it should render normally. The same happens if the omitted context helper ever returns an expiresAt that doesn't fit the trigger's bounds. The spec says an unavailable or inactive configuration keeps ordinary rendering.
findings.recommended_fix: Use a dedicated SQLSTATE or constraint-specific message for the 'scope or lifetime invalid' check. Map that code, and only that code, to the same null result as LIFETIME_UNAVAILABLE. Keep all other DB errors as PERSISTENCE_UNAVAILABLE. You could also compute expiresAt in SQL as LEAST(version.expiresAt, …), with a pre-check against clock_timestamp().
findings.required_test: On a disposable DB, set a version's expiresAt a few ms in the future (or use a fixed clock) so the trigger lifetime check fails during issue. Confirm that issueMetricVisitPage returns null, that no row persists, and that unrelated DB failures still throw.

findings.area: issueMetricVisitPage catch block; page.tsx metricPage gating
findings.issue: Only the SCOPE_UNAVAILABLE and LIFETIME_UNAVAILABLE MetricVisitorError codes return null. Every other error, including expected business-state codes the context helper may raise (runtime or readiness unavailable, fingerprint changed), is rewritten to PERSISTENCE_UNAVAILABLE and thrown. The page decides whether to call the helper using the app-clock serverNow (runtime.state !== 'unavailable'). The helper checks runtime and readiness against the DB clock.
findings.evidence: if(error instanceof MetricVisitorError&&['SCOPE_UNAVAILABLE','LIFETIME_UNAVAILABLE'].includes(error.code))return null; throw new MetricVisitorError('PERSISTENCE_UNAVAILABLE'); page: runtime = resolveLiveRuntime(..., serverNow) where serverNow = new Date().
findings.impact: Clock skew at the replay-expiry or start boundary, or a concurrent live edit between the page read and the issue transaction, can turn a page that could render normally into a 500 error page. The task allows throwing only on unexpected DB failure. Whether this happens depends on which codes the omitted context helper throws.
findings.recommended_fix: List the expected non-persistence codes from resolveMetricVisitContext and return null (render without a collector, no nonce) for runtime, readiness or context-changed states. Reserve PERSISTENCE_UNAVAILABLE for real DB or transaction failures. Alternatively, document that the helper only ever throws the two listed codes.
findings.required_test: Disposable-DB test: make the app clock see the replay as available while the DB clock sees it as expired, or change the live between the page read and the issue call. Assert the page renders without LiveMetricVisit and without a 500, and that no LiveMetricVisitPage row is committed.

findings.issue: Every anonymous GET of a public live page now runs a write transaction that locks the Live, Video and version rows (version-first, through the context helper) and inserts a row. Direct DELETE is denied and rows are kept until the version is deleted. Nothing limits how many page rows are issued and nothing prunes expired rows. Any failure, including the 5 s statement or lock timeout, throws and fails the page.
findings.evidence: INSERT INTO "LiveMetricVisitPage" on every render where the keyring is set and runtime is available; the transaction has statement_timeout 5000, timeout 10000, maxWait 5000; failures are converted to a thrown PERSISTENCE_UNAVAILABLE. The task states the rows are immutable until version deletion, and HTTP rate controls apply only to the collect endpoint.
findings.impact: Crawler, bot or flood traffic grows the table with no bound, by design never counted. If the helper takes exclusive version locks, concurrent renders queue on the same row and timeouts become public-page 500s, so a metrics outage becomes a page outage. Severity depends on the lock mode in the omitted helper.
findings.recommended_fix: Scope proposal: confirm the helper uses FOR SHARE or FOR KEY SHARE, not FOR UPDATE, on the version row for page issue. Add a privileged retention job, or allow deleting expired rows, with owner approval. Consider a render-side rate or sampling guard. The fail-closed throw is owner-specified, so keep it unless the owner decides otherwise.
findings.required_test: Concurrent page-issue test on a disposable DB (for example 50 parallel issues on one version). Assert no lock-timeout failures within budget, and measure the row growth rate.

findings.area: collect() / void collect() and the setTimeout retry
findings.issue: collect() awaits client.collect() with no try/catch. If the client ever rejects instead of returning a status, the result is an unhandled promise rejection and no retry happens.
findings.evidence: async function collect(){ const result = await client.collect(); ... } void collect(); timer = setTimeout(() => { void collect(); }, ...)
findings.impact: Collection may stop silently and unhandled-rejection noise may appear in the browser, but only if the omitted client contract allows rejection. Visit counts are not inflated.
findings.recommended_fix: Wrap the await in try/catch and treat a throw as a retryable failure, or document and test that createMetricVisitClient().collect never rejects.
findings.required_test: Unit test: mock client.collect to reject. Assert there is no unhandled rejection and the bounded retry or stop behaviour holds.

findings.area: issueMetricVisitPage: advisory lock + catch block (PERSISTENCE_UNAVAILABLE rethrow)
findings.issue: The cap fix makes one advisory lock per live a choke point on the anonymous page-render path. All issuers for a live run one at a time. Each holds the lock while it resolves the context twice, counts twice (app and trigger), inserts and re-selects. Waiters sit on a pooled connection until `statement_timeout` (5s) expires, and a lock-wait timeout falls through to `throw new MetricVisitorError('PERSISTENCE_UNAVAILABLE')` instead of returning null like the over-cap and scope-unavailable paths do.
findings.evidence: `SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtextextended(jsonb_build_array('wp20_metric_visit_page',vendorId,liveId)...))` runs first in every issuance transaction. The lock is held until commit, and the trigger re-takes the same key. The catch block only returns null for MetricVisitorError SCOPE/LIFETIME, the expired-page error and P2010/P2090. Code 57014 (statement timeout) and 55P03 (lock timeout) are rethrown. The code comments say the renderer awaits issuance before exposing the nonce.
findings.impact: A traffic burst on one popular live page queues renders behind the lock. Each waiting render holds a Prisma pool connection, which can starve unrelated requests. Requests that time out make the public page fail (if the renderer passes this error through) instead of rendering without the collector. Before this fix, issuance had no per-live lock, so this availability risk is new. Load testing is a disclosed open item, but this design choice should be visible now.
findings.recommended_fix: Keep the lock, but bound how long a render can wait. Options: use `pg_try_advisory_xact_lock`, or set a short `lock_timeout` (for example 200–500ms) before taking the lock. Map lock-unavailable or timeout (55P03/57014 from this step only) to a stamped-loss-or-null result, using the same no-collector page as the over-cap path, without releasing a nonce. Alternatively, write down an explicit throughput/pool budget per live. Also consider replacing the per-render `count(*)` with a counter row that is locked by the same key.
findings.required_test: Disposable DB: hold the per-live advisory lock in one session, start N concurrent `issueMetricVisitPage` calls for the same live, and assert they finish within the chosen bound. Assert no nonce is returned for a row that didn't commit, the page renders without the collector (or the documented behavior happens), and pool connections are released. Add a test that other lives are not blocked.

findings.area: issueMetricVisitPage over-cap branch (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE / UPDATE lossAt)
findings.issue: After the first loss stamp, every later over-cap render still runs `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on the earliest row and then an UPDATE that changes nothing.
findings.evidence: `ORDER BY "issuedAt","eventId" LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE` runs without checking whether any `lossAt` is already set. The UPDATE is filtered by `"lossAt" IS NULL`, so it matches no rows after the first stamp.
findings.impact: Each capped render does extra row locking and writing. It also briefly conflicts with a prepare holding `FOR SHARE` on that earliest event. Correctness is not affected.
findings.recommended_fix: Before locking, check whether a stamp already exists (`SELECT 1 ... WHERE versionId=... AND "lossAt" IS NOT NULL LIMIT 1`) and return null right away if it does. Only lock and stamp when no stamp exists yet. The advisory lock already serializes this.
findings.required_test: Disposable DB at the cap: the first over-cap issue stamps exactly one row, and later issues return null without row locks or updates. Verify with `pg_locks` or statement counts, and check that `lossAt` doesn't change.

findings.area: issueMetricVisitPage transaction + catch block; src/app/(viewer)/live/[slug]/page.tsx metricPage await
findings.issue: Any issuance failure other than the allowed null paths throws MetricVisitorError('PERSISTENCE_UNAVAILABLE') out of PublicLivePage, so the whole public live page errors. One cause is waiting behind the per-live advisory lock. Under a render burst for one live, waiting issuers also hold pooled DB connections.
findings.evidence: Every page render where the keyring is set and the state is not 'unavailable' runs `pg_advisory_xact_lock(...)` keyed only by vendorId/liveId, with `statement_timeout` 5000 ms, transaction timeout 10000 ms and maxWait 5000 ms. All renders for one live are serialized across context resolution, count, insert, a second context resolution and requireMetricVisitPage. The catch block converts lock or statement timeouts, P2028 and pool waits into a thrown PERSISTENCE_UNAVAILABLE. page.tsx awaits this call without a guard. The collector's own comment says it 'never changes playback'.
findings.impact: For a popular live with collection set up, enough concurrent renders queue on one advisory lock while each holds a pooled connection. They can hit the 5 s statement timeout, pool maxWait or the transaction timeout and return a page error instead of the ordinary page, and they can starve other DB queries of connections. This is a deliberate fail-closed choice (no silent untracked page). Even so, a failure in the analytics path can take the public page down, and the source does not limit that exposure.
findings.recommended_fix: Make the trade-off explicit and bounded. For example, use a short, separate lock-wait budget (such as pg_try_advisory_xact_lock or a lock_timeout well under the page budget). On contention, record the loss through the same permitted lossAt null→DB-time update, or a dedicated loss counter, in a small separate transaction, then render the ordinary page without the collector. Throw only when even recording the loss fails. Otherwise, document and test that failing the page is the intended behavior.
findings.required_test: Disposable DB test: hold the advisory lock for one live from a separate session past the lock budget, then render or issue. Assert the documented outcome: either an ordinary page without collector plus a recorded loss, or the intentional error. Assert that other DB-backed pages are not starved for pool connections during the wait.

findings.issue: The original error is discarded when it is rethrown as PERSISTENCE_UNAVAILABLE.
findings.evidence: `throw new MetricVisitorError('PERSISTENCE_UNAVAILABLE')` has no cause and no sanitized log of the Prisma code or SQLSTATE. The page-level 404 paths, by contrast, log codes.
findings.impact: Operators cannot tell a cap-trigger violation, an advisory-lock timeout, a P2028 transaction timeout, a context-change mismatch or a post-insert lookup mismatch apart. Debugging the public page error described above is harder as a result.
findings.recommended_fix: Log a non-PII classification (error class, Prisma code, meta.code SQLSTATE, or an internal marker such as 'context changed') before rethrowing, or attach it as `cause` without persisting or exposing it to the browser.
findings.required_test: Unit test: force a timeout or unknown error in the transaction and assert that a sanitized classification is logged and that no secret, URL or identity value appears in the log.

findings.area: issueMetricVisitPage cap check (usage.count>=MAX_METRIC_VISIT_PAGES) together with migration trigger cap check (>=10000)
findings.issue: The per-version cap never frees up: expired rows and rows that were never matched still count toward it. Any anonymous page render inserts a row, so a client with no identity (or just normal traffic above 10000 renders per version) can permanently turn off collection for that version.
findings.evidence: The count query has no filter on expiresAt or on whether the row was matched. The trigger counts every row for the version. By design nothing can delete or reclaim rows. Issuance runs on the public render path, before any visitor identity and before the collect-side rate limits the collection docstring says the HTTP boundary must enforce.
findings.impact: Data stays correct (the loss is stamped and completeness is not faked), but availability does not: once the cap is reached, every later render for the version goes untracked for the rest of its life, and a cheap anonymous burst can cause this early. This is an inherent trade-off of the chosen fix, so it may be better handled as a scope proposal than a regression.
findings.recommended_fix: Rate-limit or otherwise gate issuance per client before the transaction runs. Alternatively, add a database-enforced way to fold expired, unmatched expectations into an append-only per-version loss or uncounted counter, so space can be reclaimed without hiding the gap. In either case, document 10000 renders per version as a hard product limit.
findings.required_test: On a disposable database, run 10000 anonymous issuances for one version and confirm that every later render returns null with the loss stamped. Then check that whatever gating or aggregation is chosen stops exhaustion by a single client, and that the aggregated loss count stays accurate.

findings.issue: The database allows a loss stamp on any row, at any time, on as many rows as anyone likes. It does not check that the version has reached the cap or that the stamped row is the first one. The rule that loss is marked only at the cap, on the first row, is enforced only in the app. The marker also sits on an ordinary page-expectation row that can still be matched later.
findings.evidence: The UPDATE branch checks only OLD.lossAt IS NULL, NEW.lossAt IS NOT NULL, and that no other column changed. Unlike the INSERT path, it does not take the advisory lock or count rows.
findings.impact: This errs on the conservative side, since it can only report less completeness, never more. But a future reader that treats lossAt as a property of a single row, or that expects exactly one marker, could misread the data. There is no current integrity risk because no grants exist.
findings.recommended_fix: Either have the guard require the advisory lock, a count at or above the cap, and that the target is the first row, or document that any non-null lossAt on any row means the whole version is incomplete from the earliest lossAt onward. That rule should then hold for future readers.
findings.required_test: As the owning role, run a direct SQL UPDATE that sets lossAt on a non-first row below the cap. Check that it is either rejected or handled by the documented version-level reading rule in reader tests.
